title: Internet Basics
short: What the internet is, how it started and what it is built out of.
lede: Definitions you can quote word-for-word. This chapter is where the vocabulary for the whole unit comes from.
lens: Definitions, one-mark factual questions and the history of the internet.
**The terms you learn here reappear in every later chapter.**
concepts: **1. What the internet is.** The internet is a **worldwide network of networks** — millions of smaller networks joined together so that any computer can reach any other. It is not owned by any single organisation; it runs on shared standards called **protocols**.

**2. How it began.** It grew out of **ARPANET**, started in **1969** by the US Department of Defense's research agency. The first message travelled between UCLA and Stanford. India connected to the internet on **15 August 1995** through VSNL. The **World Wide Web**, invented by **Tim Berners-Lee in 1989**, is what made the internet usable by ordinary people — the web is *part of* the internet, not the same thing as it.

**3. The building blocks.** A **client** requests something, a **server** supplies it. An **ISP (Internet Service Provider)** gives you the connection — Airtel, Jio, BSNL. A **host** is any computer permanently attached to the internet with its own address. **Bandwidth** is how much data can move per second; **latency** is how long a request takes to arrive.

**4. Addressing.** Every device on the internet has an **IP address** (for example `192.168.1.5`). Because numbers are hard to remember, **DNS (Domain Name System)** translates names like `clickalex.github.io` into IP addresses. **IPv4** uses 32 bits, which ran out — **IPv6** uses 128 bits and is the replacement.
tricks: - **ARPANET 1969, Berners-Lee 1989, India 1995.** Three dates, three marks.
- **Web ≠ internet.** The web is one service running *on* the internet, like email and FTP.
- **DNS = the internet's phone book.** Names in, IP addresses out.
- **IPv4 = 32 bits, IPv6 = 128 bits.** The number of bits is the whole difference you are asked about.
mistakes: - Calling the **World Wide Web** the same thing as the internet — the web is a service on it.
- Writing that the internet has a single owner or central controller — it does not.

qa.q: When did India first get internet access, and through which provider?
qa.a: India got internet access on **15 August 1995**, through **VSNL (Videsh Sanchar Nigam Limited)**.

qa.q: What is the internet? Give two of its features.
qa.a: The internet is a worldwide network of networks in which millions of smaller networks are interconnected, allowing any computer to communicate with any other. Two of its features are: it has **no single owner or central control**, running instead on shared protocols; and it provides **many services at once** — the World Wide Web, email, file transfer and video calls all travel over the same infrastructure.

qa.q: What was ARPANET and why is it important?
qa.a: ARPANET (Advanced Research Projects Agency Network) was started in **1969** by the US Department of Defense's research agency. It is important because it was the **first packet-switched network** and the direct ancestor of today's internet — its first connection ran between UCLA and Stanford Research Institute.

qa.q: What is the role of DNS?
qa.a: **DNS (Domain Name System)** translates human-readable domain names such as `clickalex.github.io` into the numeric **IP addresses** that computers actually use to find each other. Without it, users would have to memorise numbers like `140.82.121.4` to reach any website. DNS works like a distributed phone book for the internet.

qa.q: What is the internet and how did it begin?
qa.a: The internet is a worldwide network of networks that links millions of computers using the TCP/IP family of protocols. It began in 1969 as ARPANET, a project of the US Department of Defense that linked four university computers, and grew into the public network we use after the World Wide Web was invented in 1989.

qa.q: Distinguish between IPv4 and IPv6.
qa.a: **IPv4** uses **32-bit** addresses, giving roughly 4.3 billion possible addresses — written as four numbers separated by dots, such as `192.168.1.5`. **IPv6** uses **128-bit** addresses, written in hexadecimal groups such as `2001:0db8:85a3::8a2e:0370:7334`. IPv6 was created because the supply of IPv4 addresses was exhausted by the growth in connected devices; it also has better built-in support for security and automatic configuration.

qa.q: Explain the terms World Wide Web, webpage, website and homepage.
a: The World Wide Web is the collection of linked documents and resources reached over the internet, invented by Tim Berners-Lee.
A webpage is a single document, written in HTML, that a browser displays.
A website is a group of related webpages stored under one domain name, such as a school's site with pages for admissions, results and contact.
The homepage is the first page that opens when you visit a website, from which the other pages are reached.

title: Internet Services & Protocols
short: WWW, email, FTP, chat — and the protocol behind each one.
lede: Service and protocol come as a pair. Learn them together and half the unit is memorised.
lens: Match the service to its protocol; explain what each service does.
concepts: **1. The protocol stack.** Data on the internet is layered. **HTTP/HTTPS** carries web pages, **TCP** makes sure every part of a message arrives and in the right order, and **IP** handles addressing and routing. Together they are written **TCP/IP**. **UDP** is TCP's faster, less careful cousin, used for streaming and calls where a lost packet matters less than a delay.

**2. Web services.** The **World Wide Web** is a collection of documents written in **HTML** and linked by **URLs**, fetched with **HTTP** (default port **80**) or **HTTPS** (port **443**), which adds encryption. A **URL** has three parts — the protocol (`https://`), the domain (`clickalex.github.io`) and the path (`/index.html`).

**3. Mail and files.** **Email** uses **SMTP** to send a message and **POP3** or **IMAP** to receive it; POP3 downloads and usually deletes, IMAP keeps everything on the server. **FTP (File Transfer Protocol, port 21)** moves files between machines. **Telnet (port 23)** gives a text login to a remote computer.

**4. Real-time services.** **VoIP** carries voice over the internet; **video conferencing** carries voice plus video; **instant messaging** and **chat rooms** carry text. All of these lean on UDP for speed.
tricks: - **SMTP Sends, POP Pulls, IMAP Keeps.** That one sentence settles every email-protocol question.
- **HTTP 80, HTTPS 443.** HTTPS is just HTTP inside encryption.
- **URL = protocol + domain + path.** Split any address into those three and you have answered the question.
- **TCP is careful, UDP is fast.** Reliable delivery versus live streaming.
mistakes: - Writing that **SMTP receives** email — it only sends. Receiving is POP3 or IMAP.
- Treating **HTTP and HTTPS** as different services rather than the same service with and without encryption.
- Forgetting the **port numbers** when the question asks for them.

qa.q: Give the full form of FTP and its default port.
qa.a: **FTP** stands for **File Transfer Protocol**, and its default port is **21**. It is used to upload and download files between a client and a server.

qa.q: What is the difference between HTTP and HTTPS?
qa.a: **HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol)** is the protocol used to fetch web pages, and it sends everything in plain text on port **80**. **HTTPS** is the same protocol wrapped in encryption using TLS/SSL, on port **443**. The practical difference is that with HTTPS a third party watching the network cannot read or alter the data — which is why banking and login pages always use it.

qa.q: Explain the difference between POP3 and IMAP.
qa.a: Both protocols receive email, but they handle storage differently. **POP3** downloads messages to your device and normally deletes them from the server, so the mail is only on that one machine. **IMAP** leaves messages on the server and synchronises, so the same mailbox looks identical on a phone, a laptop and a web browser. IMAP needs a constant connection and server space; POP3 works offline once downloaded.

qa.q: What is the difference between TCP and UDP?
qa.a: **TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)** is connection-oriented: it checks that every packet arrived and reorders them, so delivery is guaranteed but slightly slower. **UDP (User Datagram Protocol)** simply sends packets without checking, so it is faster but some data may be lost. TCP is used for web pages and email, where a missing piece breaks the result; UDP is used for live video, VoIP and gaming, where a small loss is better than a delay.

qa.q: Match each service with the protocol it uses: browsing the web, sending email, reading email, transferring files.
qa.a: Browsing uses HTTP or HTTPS; sending email uses SMTP; reading email uses POP3 or IMAP; transferring files uses FTP. DNS is not a service but the system that converts a domain name into an IP address so that the service can find the right computer.

qa.q: Break down the parts of this URL: `https://clickalex.github.io/IT-402-/index.html`.
qa.a: The URL has three parts. **`https://`** is the protocol — it says the page will be fetched securely over HTTPS on port 443. **`clickalex.github.io`** is the domain name, which DNS resolves into an IP address. **`/IT-402-/index.html`** is the path, pointing to a specific file inside the `IT-402-` folder on that server.

title: Network Types, Topologies & Devices
short: LAN to WAN, star to ring, and the boxes in between.
lede: Topology questions ask for a diagram plus one advantage and one disadvantage. Prepare both.
lens: Classify a network by its size, identify a topology from a description, name a device's job.
concepts: **1. Networks by size.** A **LAN (Local Area Network)** covers a room or a building — a school lab. A **MAN (Metropolitan Area Network)** covers a city — a cable TV network. A **WAN (Wide Area Network)** covers countries or the world; **the internet is the largest WAN**. A **PAN (Personal Area Network)** is the smallest, joining devices around one person, usually by Bluetooth.

**2. Topologies — the shape of the wiring.** **Bus**: one central cable with all nodes attached; cheap but if the main cable fails everything stops. **Star**: every node connects to a central hub or switch; a single cable failing only drops one node, but the centre is a single point of failure. **Ring**: nodes form a closed loop, data travelling one way; easy to add nodes, but a break stops the ring. **Mesh**: every node links to several others, giving the highest reliability at the highest cost. **Tree** combines stars in a hierarchy.

**3. Transmission media.** **Wired** — twisted-pair cable (RJ-45 connector, common in LANs), coaxial cable, and **optical fibre**, which carries light and is the fastest and least affected by interference. **Wireless** — Wi-Fi (IEEE **802.11**), Bluetooth, infrared, and satellite links.

**4. Devices.** A **hub** repeats a signal to every port and cannot tell machines apart. A **switch** learns which device sits on which port and sends data only there — this is why switches replaced hubs. A **router** joins different networks and chooses the best path, working at the network layer. A **modem** converts digital signals to analog and back so data can travel over telephone or cable lines. A **repeater** simply boosts a weakening signal. A **gateway** connects networks that use different protocols. A **NIC (Network Interface Card)** is what physically attaches a computer to the network; every NIC has a unique **MAC address**.
tricks: - **PAN < LAN < MAN < WAN.** Smallest to largest.
- **Star is the safest single-node failure, mesh the safest overall, bus the cheapest.**
- **Hub shouts, switch whispers, router chooses.** One line for all three.
- **Optical fibre = light = fastest + no electrical interference.**
mistakes: - Confusing **hub and switch** — a hub broadcasts to all ports, a switch sends only to the intended one.
- Confusing **router and modem** — a modem converts signals, a router routes between networks.
- Answering a topology question without naming **one advantage and one disadvantage**.
- Writing **MAC address** when the question asks for **IP address** — MAC is fixed to the hardware, IP is assigned to the network.

qa.q: Which IEEE standard defines Wi-Fi?
qa.a: **IEEE 802.11** defines Wi-Fi. The IEEE 802.3 standard, by contrast, defines wired Ethernet.

qa.q: Why is optical fibre preferred over copper cable for long distances?
qa.a: Optical fibre carries data as **pulses of light** through glass, so it suffers almost no signal loss over long distances and is **immune to electrical interference** from motors, power lines and lightning. It also has a far higher bandwidth than copper. Its drawbacks are that it is more expensive and more fragile to install, which is why copper still dominates the last few metres.

qa.q: What is the difference between a MAC address and an IP address?
qa.a: A **MAC address** is a 48-bit hardware address burnt into the network card; it never changes and identifies the physical device. An **IP address** is assigned logically for the network the device is on, so it changes when the device moves to a different network. MAC works within one local network, while IP works across the whole internet.

qa.q: Distinguish between a LAN and a WAN.
qa.a: A LAN covers a small area such as a room, a building or a campus, is owned by one organisation, uses switches and cables or Wi-Fi, and is fast. A WAN covers a city, a country or the world, links LANs over leased telephone lines, fibre or satellites, and is slower and shared among many organisations.

qa.q: Explain star topology with its advantages and disadvantages.
qa.a: In **star topology** every node is connected by its own cable to a central device — a hub or a switch. All communication passes through that centre. Its **advantages** are that a cable failure affects only the one node attached to it, nodes can be added or removed without disturbing the rest, and faults are easy to locate. Its **disadvantages** are that it needs more cable than a bus, and the central device is a **single point of failure** — if the switch dies, the whole network stops.

qa.q: Differentiate between a hub, a switch and a router.
qa.a: A **hub** works at the physical layer and repeats an incoming signal out of every port, so all devices see all traffic and collisions are common. A **switch** works at the data-link layer, learns the MAC address on each port and forwards a frame only to the intended port, which makes it far faster and more secure. A **router** works at the network layer and connects *different* networks, using IP addresses to choose the best path between them — it is what links your LAN to the internet.

a: Idea: LAN to WAN, star to ring, and the boxes in between..

In star topology every node is connected by its own cable to a central device — a hub or a switch. All communication passes through that centre. Its advantages are that a cable failure affects only the one node attached to it, nodes can be added or removed without disturbing the rest, and faults are easy to locate. Its disadvantages are that it needs more cable than a bus, and the central device is a single point of failure — if the switch dies, the whole network stops.

qa.q: Compare the star and bus topologies and name one advantage of each.
a: In a star topology every computer is connected to a central switch or hub; a fault in one cable affects only that computer, and new computers can be added easily.
In a bus topology all computers share one main cable with terminators at each end; it is cheap and needs less cable.
Star costs more because of the switch and the extra cable, while bus is slow when many computers share the cable and stops working if the main cable breaks.
Star is the topology used in almost every modern office network.

Two students attempt: “Explain star topology with its advantages and disadvantages.” Student A writes one line. Student B writes points, an example and a check.

(a) Which answer frame should you use for full marks?
(b) Write the model points.
(c) Add one memory trick you would use on exam morning.
a: (a) Statement → working or reasons in points → example or check. One-line answers lose step marks.

(b) In star topology every node is connected by its own cable to a central device — a hub or a switch. All communication passes through that centre. Its advantages are that a cable failure affects only the one node attached to it, nodes can be added or removed without disturbing the rest, and faults are easy to locate. Its disadvantages are that it needs more cable than a bus, and the central device is a single point of failure — if the switch dies, the whole network stops.
(c) PAN < LAN < MAN < WAN. Smallest to largest.

qa.q: Discuss “Network Types, Topologies & Devices” in detail. Include the idea that carries marks, one worked example or answer frame, and why students lose marks.
a: Networks by size. A LAN (Local Area Network) covers a room or a building — a school lab. A MAN (Metropolitan Area Network) covers a city — a cable TV network. A WAN (Wide Area Network) covers countries or the world; the internet is the largest WAN. A PAN (Personal Area Network) is the smallest, joining devices around one person, usually by Bluetooth.
Marks lens: Classify a network by its size, identify a topology from a description, name a device's job.
Method / memory trick: PAN < LAN < MAN < WAN. Smallest to largest.
Do not: Confusing hub and switch — a hub broadcasts to all ports, a switch sends only to the intended one.

mcq.q: Which network covers a whole city? (a) LAN (b) MAN (c) WAN (d) PAN
mcq.a: **(b) MAN** — Metropolitan Area Network.

mcq.q: Which topology has a single point of failure at its centre? (a) Mesh (b) Bus (c) Star (d) Ring
mcq.a: **(c) Star** — the hub or switch is the single point of failure.

mcq.q: A device that joins two different networks and picks the best path is a — (a) hub (b) switch (c) repeater (d) router
mcq.a: **(d) router.**

mcq.q: Which medium is immune to electrical interference? (a) twisted pair (b) coaxial (c) optical fibre (d) infrared
mcq.a: **(c) optical fibre** — it carries light, not electricity.

mcq.q: The most exam-ready way to revise “Network Types, Topologies & Devices” is: (a) read the heading only  (b) learn the key idea plus one example  (c) skip written practice  (d) memorise a random extra topic
mcq.a: **(b) learn the key idea plus one example.** The chapter is LAN to WAN, star to ring, and the boxes in between..

mcq.q: A 3-mark answer on “Network Types, Topologies & Devices” should: (a) be one sentence  (b) start with the idea, then a reason or method  (c) copy the whole chapter  (d) leave the example out
mcq.a: **(b) start with the idea, then a reason or method.** Step marks follow that frame.

mcq.q: The device that connects two different networks and chooses the best path is a: (a) router  (b) switch  (c) hub  (d) repeater
mcq.a: **(a) router.** A switch connects computers within one network; a repeater only strengthens the signal.

mcq.q: The topology in which every computer is connected to every other computer is the: (a) mesh topology  (b) star topology  (c) bus topology  (d) ring topology
mcq.a: **(a) mesh topology.** It is the most reliable and the most expensive to cable.

trend: One topology question with a diagram, plus a device-comparison question, appears in most papers.
onepager: - PAN < LAN < MAN < WAN.
- Star: safe per node, fragile at the centre. Bus: cheapest, fragile cable. Mesh: most reliable, most expensive.
- Hub broadcasts, switch forwards to one port, router joins networks, modem converts signals.
- Twisted pair (RJ-45), coaxial, optical fibre; wireless = 802.11, Bluetooth, infrared.
- MAC = hardware, IP = network.
task: Draw star, bus and ring topology in your file. Under each write one advantage and one disadvantage. This is exactly what the exam asks for.
formulas: LAN < MAN < WAN < the Internet — by area covered
Topologies: **bus** (one cable), **star** (all to a hub/switch), **ring** (each to the next), **mesh** (every node to many)
Devices: **hub** repeats to all · **switch** sends to one · **router** joins networks · **modem** converts the signal
Transmission media: twisted pair, coaxial, fibre optic (guided); radio, microwave, satellite (unguided)
steps: 1. Decide the **area** the network covers — a room, a campus, or a country.
2. Draw the **topology** in words: what sits at the centre, and what happens if it fails.
3. Choose the **device for each job** — switch inside a network, router between networks.
4. Pick the **medium** on cost, distance and interference, and state the reason for the choice.

title: Mobile & Wireless Technology
short: Generations from 1G to 5G, plus the short-range wireless around you.
lede: One table, learnt properly, answers every generation question.
lens: Compare generations, name short-range technologies and their uses.
**Generations are a table question — memorise the table.**
concepts: **1. Mobile generations.** **1G** was analog and voice-only. **2G** went digital and added **SMS** and basic data through **GPRS**. **3G** made mobile internet genuinely usable — video calls and browsing at a few Mbps. **4G/LTE** is all-IP and built for data, giving tens of Mbps and making video streaming normal. **5G** targets speeds up to around 20 Gbps with latency under a millisecond, which is what makes remote surgery, autonomous vehicles and dense IoT possible.

**2. Short-range wireless.** **Bluetooth** joins devices a few metres apart — headphones, keyboards, file sharing. **Wi-Fi** covers a building using the **IEEE 802.11** family of standards. **Infrared** needs a clear line of sight and is used in remote controls. **NFC** works within a few centimetres and is what contactless payments and transit cards use.

**3. Mobile data plumbing.** A phone talks to a **cell tower**; the area one tower covers is a **cell**, and handover moves a call from one cell to the next without dropping it. **Roaming** is what lets a phone work on another operator's network when you travel.
**4. Why it matters.** Each generation did not just get faster — it changed what phones could do. 2G added text, 3G added the web, 4G added video, 5G adds machines talking to machines.
tricks: - **1 voice → 2 text → 3 web → 4 video → 5 machines.** Five words for five generations.
- **Bluetooth = metres, Wi-Fi = a building, cell tower = kilometres.**
- **NFC needs centimetres** — that is why you tap, not wave.
- **Handover** keeps a call alive as you drive between cells.
mistakes: - Saying 4G is faster *only* — it is also **all-IP**, which is the point.
- Confusing **Bluetooth and NFC** ranges: Bluetooth is metres, NFC is centimetres.
- Forgetting that **infrared needs line of sight**, unlike Bluetooth and Wi-Fi.

qa.q: What is the difference between Bluetooth and NFC?
qa.a: **Bluetooth** works over a range of a few metres and is used for continuous connections such as headphones, speakers and keyboards. **NFC (Near Field Communication)** works only within a few centimetres and is used for a single quick exchange — contactless payments, transit cards, pairing by tapping. Bluetooth needs pairing; NFC works by simply bringing two devices together.

qa.q: What is a cell and what is handover?
qa.a: A **cell** is the geographic area covered by one mobile tower. A whole city is divided into many cells, which is why mobile networks are called cellular. **Handover** is the automatic process of moving an ongoing call or data session from one cell's tower to the next as the user travels, so the connection does not drop.

qa.q: Why does infrared need line of sight but Wi-Fi does not?
qa.a: Infrared uses **light waves**, which cannot pass through solid objects, so the transmitter and receiver must see each other directly — that is why a TV remote only works when pointed at the TV. Wi-Fi uses **radio waves**, which pass through walls and furniture, so it works throughout a building without a direct line of sight.

qa.q: What does 4G mean and how is it better than 3G?
qa.a: 4G is the fourth generation of mobile network technology, designed for data rather than voice, with download speeds of up to about 100 Mbps, smooth video streaming and low delay. 3G was built mainly to improve voice calls and gave only modest data speeds, so tasks such as video calling were slow or impossible.

qa.q: Compare 3G, 4G and 5G.
qa.a: **3G** made mobile internet practical, offering speeds up to about 2 Mbps, which allowed video calling and basic browsing. **4G (LTE)** is an all-IP network designed around data rather than voice, reaching around 100 Mbps and making HD video streaming and VoIP everyday features. **5G** targets up to 20 Gbps with latency below one millisecond; its real significance is not faster phones but support for **massive numbers of connected devices** — IoT sensors, autonomous vehicles and remote medical procedures.

qa.q: Riya is revising “Mobile & Wireless Technology” (Generations from 1G to 5G, plus the short-range wireless around you.). A classmate lost marks by doing this: Saying 4G is faster *only* — it is also all-IP, which is the point. Apply the correct method and rewrite the scoring answer.
a: Correct method: 1 voice → 2 text → 3 web → 4 video → 5 machines. Five words for five generations.
Why the mistake costs marks: Saying 4G is faster *only* — it is also all-IP, which is the point.
Write the definition or formula first, then the working or example.

qa.q: Amit is given this exam-style task from “Mobile & Wireless Technology”: “Compare 3G, 4G and 5G.” Treat it as an application question. Identify the idea, then write the working in points.
a: Idea: Generations from 1G to 5G, plus the short-range wireless around you..

G made mobile internet practical, offering speeds up to about 2 Mbps, which allowed video calling and basic browsing. 4G (LTE) is an all-IP network designed around data rather than voice, reaching around 100 Mbps and making HD video streaming and VoIP everyday features. 5G targets up to 20 Gbps with latency below one millisecond; its real significance is not faster phones but support for massive numbers of connected devices — IoT sensors, autonomous vehicles and remote medical procedures.

qa.q: Name four short-range wireless technologies and give one use of each.
a: Bluetooth connects a phone to wireless earphones, a keyboard or a speaker within about ten metres.
Wi-Fi connects devices to a local network and through it to the internet, at home, in school or in a cafe.
NFC allows contactless payments and data exchange when two devices are touched or held a few centimetres apart.
Infrared needs a direct line of sight and is still used in television remote controls.

qa.q: Why is 5G described as ‘for machines’ rather than just ‘faster phones’? Explain with reference to IoT and latency.
a: Speed alone would only improve video on phones, which 4G already handles well.
5G's real change is low latency plus massive device density: millions of sensors, vehicles and appliances can talk to each other in milliseconds.
That is what the Internet of Things needs — a driverless car or a factory robot cannot wait for a slow round-trip. Hence: 1 voice, 2 text, 3 web, 4 video, 5 machines.

title: Web Browsers, Search & Web Concepts
short: Browsers, search engines, cookies, caching and the difference between a web page and a website.
lede: Short chapter, high mark density. Mostly one- and two-mark definitions.
lens: Define terms, compare browsers with search engines, explain cookies and caching.
**This chapter closes Unit I — revise it as one block.**
concepts: **1. Browser versus search engine.** A **web browser** (Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari) is *software on your device* that requests and displays pages. A **search engine** (Google, Bing) is *a website* that indexes other websites so you can find them. You use a browser to reach a search engine — they are not alternatives to each other.

**2. Pages, sites and home pages.** A **web page** is a single HTML document. A **website** is a collection of related pages under one domain. The **home page** is the entry page, usually `index.html`. A **web portal** gathers links, news and services in one place.

**3. Cookies and cache.** A **cookie** is a small piece of data a website stores in your browser to remember you — a login, a language, the contents of a cart. **Caching** stores a local copy of a page or image so it loads faster and uses less bandwidth the next time. **Browsing history** is the record of pages visited. All three raise privacy questions, which is why browsers now offer private modes.

**4. Finding things.** A **search engine** uses a **crawler** (or spider) to visit pages, an **index** to store what it found, and a **ranking algorithm** to order results. **Bookmarking** saves an address you want to return to; **RSS feeds** push updates from a site to you instead of you checking it.
tricks: - **Browser is on your machine; search engine is on the web.**
- **Cookie remembers you, cache speeds you up, history records you.** Three different things, three different questions.
- **Crawler visits → index stores → algorithm ranks.**
- A **website** is many pages; a **web page** is one document.
mistakes: - Calling Google a **browser** — it is a search engine, a website.
- Confusing **cookies with cache** — cookies are identity data, cache is a speed copy.
- Saying a **home page** is the same as a **web page** in general — the home page is specifically the entry page.

qa.q: Name any three web browsers.
qa.a: **Google Chrome**, **Mozilla Firefox** and **Microsoft Edge**. Apple's **Safari** and **Opera** are other common examples.

qa.q: Differentiate between a web browser and a search engine.
qa.a: A **web browser** is software installed on your computer or phone — Chrome, Firefox, Edge or Safari — that sends requests for pages and renders the HTML it receives into the page you see. A **search engine** such as Google is itself a website whose job is to index other websites and return a ranked list of results for your query. You need a browser in order to open a search engine, so they work together rather than as alternatives.

qa.q: What are cookies and why are they used?
qa.a: A **cookie** is a small piece of data that a website stores in the user's browser. Websites use cookies to remember something about the user between visits — whether they are logged in, which language they chose, or what is in their shopping cart. Without cookies, every page request would be treated as a brand-new visitor. Because cookies can also be used to track browsing behaviour, browsers offer private modes that discard them when the window closes.

qa.q: What is caching and what is its benefit?
qa.a: **Caching** means keeping a local copy of a resource — a page, an image or a stylesheet — so that it does not have to be downloaded again. The benefits are that pages **load faster** and **use less bandwidth**, which matters most on slow or metered connections. The trade-off is that a cached copy can be out of date, which is why a forced refresh sometimes shows a different page.

qa.q: How does a search engine find and rank pages?
qa.a: A search engine uses a **crawler** — also called a spider — that automatically visits web pages and follows the links on them to discover more. What it finds is stored in an **index**, a huge searchable catalogue. When you type a query, a **ranking algorithm** scores the matching pages by relevance, authority and quality, and returns them in order.

qa.q: What is the difference between a web browser and a search engine?
qa.a: A browser is the program that requests, receives and displays web pages — Chrome, Firefox, Edge or Safari. A search engine is a website, such as Google or Bing, that keeps an index of pages and returns a list of results for your query. The browser is the tool you use; the search engine is a site you visit with it.

A web browser is software installed on your computer or phone — Chrome, Firefox, Edge or Safari — that sends requests for pages and renders the HTML it receives into the page you see. A search engine such as Google is itself a website whose job is to index other websites and return a ranked list of results for your query. You need a browser in order to open a search engine, so they work together rather than as alternatives.

qa.q: What are cookies and cache, and why should you clear them sometimes?
a: Cookies are small files a website stores on your computer to remember who you are, what is in your basket and what your preferences are.
The cache stores copies of images, scripts and pages so that a site loads faster the next time you visit it.
Clearing them removes old or corrupted files that can make a site load wrongly, frees disk space, logs you out of accounts and limits tracking.
The cost is that you have to sign in again and the first visit to a site is slower.
